1905.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁-der.? Ancient Greek πάλαι (pálai) Ancient Greek -ος (-os) Ancient Greek παλαιός From πάλαι (pálai, “long ago”) + -ος (-os, “adjectival suffix”).

1957.t: From earlier δϝίς (dwĭ́s), from Proto-Hellenic *dwís, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís; related to δύο (dŭ́o, “two”). Cognates include the Sanskrit द्विस् (dvís) and the Latin bis and dis-.

1948.t: By surface analysis, ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow, stream, gush”) + -σις (-sĭs). Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *srútis, from *srew- (“to flow, stream”) + *-tis.

1906.t: Compound of πᾶν (pân, “everything”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”) + -ος (-os, “noun of result or an abstract noun of action”).

1964.t: Related to, and perhaps derived from, κυφός (kuphós, “bent forward, hunchbacked”), which Beekes suspects is of Pre-Greek origin; see there for more.

1903.t: From Proto-Hellenic *némō, from Proto-Indo-European *ném-e-ti (“to assign, allot; take”). Cognate with English numb, Dutch nemen, German nehmen, and Albanian njeh (“count”), nëmë (“curse”).

1902.t: The word is most probably Pre-Greek, because of its variants.

1923.t: From ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + *λῆθος (*lêthos, “*concealment”) + -ής (-ḗs). *λῆθος (*lêthos) is the neuter σ-stem abstract noun to the root of λανθάνω (lanthánō, “I am hidden”), the existence of which is warranted by its Doric variant λᾶθος (lâthos).

1919.t: From τέλος (télos, “end”) + -ιος (-ios, adjective suffix). Related to, and largely synonymous with, τελήεις (telḗeis).

1972.t: The four principal parts of the verb display the e-grade, o-grade, and zero-grade (πενθ-, πονθ-, παθ- (penth-, ponth-, path-)) of a root of uncertain identity.

1914.t: Probably Pre-Greek, but see Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ- (“to attach, fix”).

1975.t: From an earlier *στενϝός (*stenwós), of unknown further origin, with no known cognates outside Greek. According to Beekes, the suffix of the derivative στενυγρός (stenugrós, “narrow”) suggests Pre-Greek origin.

1941.t: From εἷς (heîs, “one”, masculine and neuter stem: ἑν-) + δέκατος (dékătos, “tenth”).

1931.t: From Proto-Hellenic *elə́t͏̌t͏̌ōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁léngʷʰ-yōs, from *h₁lengʷʰ- (“light (of weight)”). Synchronically ἐλαχύς (elakhús) + *-ϳων (*-jōn).

1916.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *stn̥gʰ-u-s, from a root *ste(n)gʰ- (“to stick”), and compared with Proto-Germanic *stinganą (“to sting, stick out”), Lithuanian stangùs (“fixed, stiff”), Latvian stingt (“to harden”).

1922.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂leybʰ-. Cognate with Latin lībō.

1976.t: Disputedly cognate with Middle Irish serb (“theft”), pointing to Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“to rob”), but this is uncertain.

1954.t: Either a derivative of αἴτιος (aítĭos, “causing; guilty”) or directly from unattested *αἶτος (*aîtos, “share”). In either case, from *h₂ey- (“to give”), whence also αἰτέω (aitéō, “to ask”).

1977.t: From φαίνω (phaínō, “to show, make visible, bring to light”) + -ρός (-rós).

1981.t: From ἀγαλλιάω (agalliáō), form of ἀγάλλω (agállō, “to rejoice”) + -σις (-sis).

1904.t: From earlier ὀΐομαι (oī̈́omai) and *ὀϝίομαι (*owī́omai), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew- (“perceive”).

1945.t: PIE word *h₁nómn̥ From ὀνομάζω (onomázō, “I name”) + -τός (-tós, verbal adjective suffix).

1917.t: Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *terh₃- (“to hurt”), with inchoative suffix -σκω (-skō).

1974.t: Usually derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“to curve, bend”), like σκέλος (skélos, “leg”) and σκολιός (skoliós, “bent; crooked”). The suffix -ηκ- (-ēk-) is also found in σφήξ (sphḗx, “wasp”) and μύρμηξ (múrmēx, “ant”).

1960.t: From εὐνοέω (eunoéō, “to wish well to somebody”) + -ια (-ĭă).

1921.t: From ἀδικέω (adikéō, “to behave unjustly, to commit a crime”) + -μα (-ma).

1993.t: From earlier ἐνῴδιον (enōídion), from ἐν (en) + οὖς (oûs, “ear”) + -ίδιον (-ídion). The form was later altered to re-align with ὦτα (ôtă), the plural of οὖς (oûs).

1973.t: From Proto-Indo-European *peyH- (“fat”). Cognate with Latin pīnguis (“fat; plump”) and Proto-Germanic *faitaz (“fat”).

1909.t: Univerbation of παρά (părắ) and χρῆμα (khrêmă, “matter, affair”).

1918.t: No clear etymology. Furnée connects the word with τρίβανον (tríbanon, “oil flask”), considering it to be of Pre-Greek origin.

1985.t: Unknown. The connection with Sanskrit अमीव (amīva, “pain, grief”) requires an unwarranted dissimilation m-ṷ > n-ṷ and should be rejected.

1901.t: Denominative in -ύνω (-ū́nō), like παλύνω (pălū́nō, “to bestrew; to besprinkle”) and φορύνω (phorū́nō, “to be mingled”), from an unattested base form.

1939.t: From ἐπι- (epi-, “on, upon, atop”) + θέμα (théma, “that which is placed or laid down”).

1992.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Ancient Greek ἐν (en) Ancient Greek ἐν- (en-) Proto-Indo-European *swep-der. Proto-Indo-European *supnós Proto-Hellenic *húpnos Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos) Proto-Indo-European *-yósder.
